introduction-the-flat-network-challenge.core: Kubernetes' network model requires every Pod to get its own IP and reach every other Pod directly without NAT, across nodes. Nodes reach Pods, and Pods see their own IP as others see it. Implementing this flat network across many hosts is the job of CNI plugins; Services, DNS, Ingress/Gateway and NetworkPolicies build on top.

first_principles.problem: Docker's default per-host bridge with NAT can't give cluster-wide, routable Pod IPs.
truths: Apps expect real IPs, not port mappings.

analogy.title: A city where every flat has a real postal address
analogy.story: Mail goes directly flat to flat, no forwarding through building receptions.
analogy.breaks: Addresses are permanent; Pod IPs change whenever Pods are replaced.

example.title: Cross-node Pod call
flow: A connects to B's IP directly

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Apps see a simple flat network.

check.q: What does the Kubernetes network model require between Pods?
check.a: Every Pod can reach every other Pod by IP without NAT.

cni-plugins-the-plumbers-of-kubernetes.core: The Container Network Interface is a spec for plugins the runtime calls when Pods are created and deleted: create the network interface (veth), assign an IP (IPAM), set routes and clean up. Popular CNIs: Calico (BGP or overlay, policies), Cilium (eBPF, policies, observability), Flannel (simple overlay), AWS VPC CNI and Azure CNI (cloud-native IPs).

first_principles.problem: Teams pick a CNI without knowing it determines performance, policy support and IP planning.
truths: Plugins differ in data path and features.
Cloud CNIs integrate with VPC networking.

analogy.title: Plumbers hired for each new flat
analogy.story: They connect pipes when someone moves in and disconnect them when they leave.
analogy.breaks: Plumbers take days; CNI setup takes milliseconds per Pod.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: See how each Pod is plumbed.

code.text:
ls /etc/cni/net.d/              # CNI config on the node
ip link | grep veth              # Pod veth pairs
cilium status                     # if using Cilium

points: Choose by data path and features.

check.q: What two main jobs does a CNI plugin perform for a new Pod?
check.a: Creating its network interface and assigning it an IP address (plus routes).

networking-modes-overlay-vs-direct-routi.core: Overlay networking (VXLAN, Geneve, IPIP) encapsulates Pod packets inside node-to-node packets, working on any underlay but adding overhead and MTU reduction. Direct routing (BGP, cloud route tables or native VPC IPs) routes Pod CIDRs natively for better performance and visibility, but needs underlay cooperation.

first_principles.problem: Pod-to-Pod throughput is lower than expected, and packets mysteriously drop due to MTU mismatches.
truths: Underlays may not know Pod routes.
derivation: **Overlay** when you can't change the underlay.
**Cloud-native IPs** (VPC CNI) for no overlay at all.

analogy.title: Envelopes inside envelopes versus direct addressing
analogy.story: Overlay wraps each letter in a courier envelope; direct routing writes the real address on it.
analogy.breaks: Extra envelopes cost paper; extra headers reduce MTU and add CPU work.

example.title: MTU fix
example.outcome: right network mode chosen and tuned.

check.q: Why must Pod MTU be lowered with VXLAN?
check.a: Encapsulation adds headers, so packets must be smaller to fit the underlay MTU.

dns-within-kubernetes-the-internal-phone.core: CoreDNS serves cluster DNS: Services get names like svc.namespace.svc.cluster.local (A/AAAA records to the ClusterIP, or Pod IPs for headless), plus SRV records for named ports. Pods' resolv.conf includes search domains and ndots:5, which causes multiple lookups for external names unless tuned. NodeLocal DNSCache cuts latency and conntrack issues.

first_principles.problem: External API calls are slow because each lookup tries five search-domain suffixes first.
truths: ndots:5 treats most names as relative.
DNS is on every request path.
derivation: Use **short names** within a namespace (api), **FQDN** across.
Add **trailing dot** or lower **ndots** for external names.

analogy.title: An internal phone directory with extension shortcuts
analogy.story: Dialling '201' works inside, but outside numbers first get tried as internal extensions.
analogy.breaks: Phone systems fail fast; DNS retries add seconds of delay.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: api.stripe.com resolved in one query, not five.

check.q: What is the full DNS name of Service 'api' in namespace 'shop'?

ingress-the-front-door.core: An Ingress resource defines HTTP(S) routing (host and path rules to Services, TLS certificates), and an Ingress controller (NGINX, Traefik, HAProxy, AWS Load Balancer Controller) implements it, typically behind one load balancer. Features beyond basics rely on controller-specific annotations, which limits portability.

first_principles.problem: Each web service needs its own public load balancer and certificate management.
truths: HTTP can be routed by host and path.

analogy.title: A hotel reception directing guests
analogy.story: One entrance; reception checks the booking and points each guest to the right room.
analogy.breaks: Receptionists are flexible; Ingress needs controller-specific annotations for anything advanced.

code.text:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata: {name: shop}
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls: [{hosts: [shop.example.com], secretName: shop-tls}]
  rules:
  - host: shop.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - {path: /api, pathType: Prefix, backend: {service: {name: api, port: {number: 80}}}}
      - {path: /, pathType: Prefix, backend: {service: {name: web, port: {number: 80}}}}

check.a: An Ingress controller running in the cluster.

the-gateway-api-ingress-evolved.core: Gateway API is Ingress's successor: role-oriented resources (GatewayClass by infra providers, Gateway by cluster operators, HTTPRoute/GRPCRoute/TCPRoute by app teams), standard features (header matching, traffic splitting, redirects, cross-namespace references via ReferenceGrant) without annotations, and support for multiple protocols.

first_principles.problem: Ingress annotations differ per controller, and app teams can't safely own routes without cluster-wide access.

analogy.title: An airport with separated responsibilities
analogy.story: The authority builds terminals, the operator runs gates and airlines manage their own flights.
analogy.breaks: Airlines can't redesign terminals, and similarly routes can only attach where Gateways allow.

check.q: Which Gateway API resource do application teams typically own?

network-policies-the-firewall-for-pods.core: NetworkPolicies select Pods by label and define allowed ingress and egress by Pod selector, namespace selector, IP block and port. Pods selected by any policy become default-deny for the specified direction. Enforcement depends on the CNI (Calico, Cilium support it; some don't). Start with default-deny and allow only what's needed.

first_principles.problem: A compromised frontend Pod can reach the database directly because all Pods can talk to all Pods.

analogy.title: Internal doors with keycard rules
analogy.story: By default doors are locked; badges list exactly which rooms each person can enter.
analogy.breaks: Doors are physical; policies only work if the CNI enforces them.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Only api Pods reach the database.

code.text:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: db-allow-api, namespace: shop}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: db}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}}]
    ports: [{port: 5432}]

check.q: What happens to traffic to a Pod once any NetworkPolicy selects it for ingress?
check.a: Only ingress explicitly allowed by some policy is permitted; everything else is denied.
